what_its_for: Phenytoin is used to prevent and control seizures (also called epilepsy). It works by calming abnormal electrical activity in the brain that causes seizures. It may also be used after brain surgery or head injury to prevent seizures.
how_to_take: Take phenytoin exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with food or milk if it upsets your stomach. Swallow extended-release capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. If you take the liquid (suspension), shake the bottle well for at least 2 minutes before each use and measure your dose carefully with a special measuring spoon or syringe — never use a regular kitchen spoon. Try to take it at the same time(s) every day to keep a steady level in your body.
dosing: Your dose depends on your age, weight, kidney and liver function, and how well the medication is working for you. Adults are often started on 100 mg three times a day, or 300 mg once daily with the extended-release form. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on blood tests. Never change your dose or stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, as stopping suddenly can cause dangerous seizures.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you miss several doses in a row, call your doctor right away because this can increase your risk of seizures.
storage: Store phenytoin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the liquid form from freezing and use it within the time frame recommended on the label. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking phenytoin — it can change the levels of the drug in your body and increase side effects. Do not start, stop, or change any other medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements without asking your doctor or pharmacist first, as many drugs interact with phenytoin. Avoid antacids containing calcium within 2 hours of taking phenytoin because they can reduce how well it is absorbed. Be careful driving or operating machinery until you know how this medication affects you, as it may cause dizziness or drowsiness. Do not stop taking phenytoin suddenly.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: more frequent or worse seizures, a skin rash (especially if blistering or peeling — this could be serious), swollen glands, fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe confusion or trouble walking, slurred speech, uncontrolled eye movements, thoughts of hurting yourself, or signs of a serious allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also contact your doctor if you notice swollen or bleeding gums, unusual hair growth, or if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant.
when_it_works: Phenytoin starts working to help prevent seizures fairly quickly once it reaches a steady level in your blood, which usually takes several days to a couple of weeks. Your doctor will check blood levels with regular tests to make sure the amount in your body is in the right range — not too low (which could allow seizures) and not too high (which could cause side effects). You may not feel any different day to day, but the medicine is working in the background to keep your brain activity stable. Do not stop taking it just because you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Phenytoin can harm an unborn baby and may cause birth defects. Talk to your doctor immediately if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Do not stop taking it on your own, as uncontrolled seizures during pregnancy are also dangerous. Use reliable birth control while on this medication. Breastfeeding: Small amounts pass into breast milk; talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits. Children: Doses are carefully calculated based on the child's weight and age; follow the doctor's instructions exactly. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as dizziness and confusion and may need lower doses. Liver disease: Phenytoin is broken down by the liver, so people with liver problems may need dose adjustments and closer monitoring.
